analysis.one_liner: Raises Social Security benefits and pays for it with payroll taxes on high earners.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would lift the cap on wages subject to Social Security payroll taxes, phasing in so that by 2020 every dollar of wages above the cap is taxed. The new revenue would fund larger benefits: a new benefit tier worth 5% of lifetime earnings above the cap, benefit formula increases that grow to 15%, and annual cost-of-living raises calculated on a price index that reflects what retirees actually buy. It was introduced by one senator, sent to the Finance Committee, and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Current and future Social Security retirees, survivors, and disability beneficiaries. The bill gives them three layers of higher benefits: a new 5% benefit tier based on earnings above the payroll tax cap, benefit formula increases that grow from 1% in 2021 to 15% by 2035, and cost-of-living adjustments pegged to a new Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers, which tracks the purchases typical of retirees. It also applies the new revenue toward Social Security's long-term financing.

how_it_helps.text: Adds a benefit tier equal to 5% of a worker's average lifetime earnings above the payroll tax cap, so people who paid Social Security taxes on wages above the cap finally get credit for them [S2][S3].
Raises the benefit formula's bend points, reaching a 15% increase for people becoming eligible in 2035 and later [S2][S3].
Switches the annual cost-of-living adjustment to a new Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers, which the Bureau of Labor Statistics would create to track spending typical of retirees [S2][S3].
Phases in taxation of wages above the contribution and benefit base from 80% in 2016 to 100% by 2020, for both employees and the self-employed, providing the revenue [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Workers and self-employed people whose earnings exceed the Social Security wage cap (about $118,500 in 2015). They would pay Social Security payroll tax on the portion of wages above the cap, phased in from 2016 and fully in effect after 2020. This falls on roughly the top decile of earners and on high-income professionals and business owners.
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers earning above the wage cap

drawbacks.text: Workers above the cap would see a payroll tax increase even though the new benefit formula gives little back to them directly, since the new 5% tier and bend-point increases are modest relative to the added tax at the highest earnings [S3].
The self-employed would bear both the employee and employer shares on income above the cap, raising their combined tax burden the most [S3].

Taxing earnings above the cap partially but crediting those earnings in the benefit formula creates a long-run interaction that critics of similar proposals note can erode the projected savings if benefit growth outpaces revenue; the bill leaves the financing balance to future Congresses [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the majority of workers who earn under the cap, the bill is a clear gain: higher benefits and a more retiree-accurate inflation index at no new cost to them. The cost lands entirely on high earners, which is the point of the design. The benefit increases are meaningful but not dramatic relative to the tax change at the top, and the bill's solvency improvement depends on the payroll tax cap staying in place as earnings at the top keep rising. Its main weakness was political: it arrived with no cosponsors and no committee interest, so its design was never tested in debate.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced in August 2015, and the committee never took it up; it died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Sen. Brian Schatz introduced the bill on August 5, 2015, as a stand-alone proposal to expand Social Security benefits paid for by taxing wages above the payroll tax cap [S1][S3].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance on August 5, 2015, the same day it was introduced [S5].
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action after the referral [S5].
The bill expired at the end of the 114th Congress on January 3, 2017, without ever receiving a vote [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High earners above the Social Security wage cap avoided the new payroll tax, and opponents of expanding Social Security taxes were spared a floor debate, because the Finance Committee never scheduled the bill for action.

for.name: Sen. Brian Schatz
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate on August 5, 2015.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over payroll taxes and Social Security
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on August 5, 2015, and never held a hearing, markup, or vote on it.

against.name: Sen. Orrin Hatch
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for committee consideration in the two sessions of the 114th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sole sponsor was a Democrat, it drew zero cosponsors from either party, and Republicans held the Senate majority and the Finance Committee chair during the 114th Congress; no vote was ever taken.

industries.note: They would pay Social Security payroll tax on wages above the cap, fully phased in by 2020. Their gains from the modest new benefit tier do not offset the added tax at high earnings.

industries.industry: High-income self-employed professionals and business owners
industries.note: Self-employment income above the cap would be taxed at the combined employee and employer rate, the largest single increase in the bill.
